title: Tenant adaptive shepherding playbook
content:
Purpose and scope

This note defines an operational and architectural approach were calling "tenant adaptive shepherding". Goal: reliably maintain SLAs for contracted customers while minimizing collateral throttling to best-effort tenants and maximizing overall cluster utilization across regions. This focuses on runtime routing decisions, quota accounting, regional affinity, and noisy-neighbor detection/mitigation.

High-level idea

Treat routing decisions as short-lived, tenant-aware contracts enforced by a distributed shepherd (control-plane + agents) that applies smoothing and progressive degradation rather than binary cutoffs. The shepherd:
- consumes signals (latency, queue depth, token consumption, KV cache miss rate, inference tail-latency)
- evaluates contract obligations and soft budgets in a policy engine
- emits per-request routing decisions or backpressure tokens to the serving plane
- records actions in an append-only quota ledger for audit and billing reconciliation

Why "shepherding"? Because noisy or bursty tenants need guidance (smoothing, staged model downshifts) rather than blunt ejection. Shepherding aims to keep customer experience acceptable while preserving SLA guarantees for premium tenants.

Control plane components (roles and responsibilities)

1) Policy Store (central): canonical per-tenant contract metadata and tier definitions. Contains: committed throughput, latency SLO, allowed model families, regional pins, billing flags.

2) Decision Engine (global but sharded): evaluates policy + telemetry to produce routing directives. Lightweight policy language (see example snippet below) supports time-windowed budgets, emergency headroom, and progressive fallback chains.

3) Quota Ledger: append-only log of allocations and enforced throttles. Used for reconciliation with billing and for replay during incident investigation.

4) Local Shepherd Agent (per-region agent co-located with serving nodes): consumes local telemetry (GPU load, queue lengths, KV cache metrics), queries Decision Engine caches, enforces local per-tenant leaky buckets, and orchestrates graceful model downgrades.

5) Telemetry and Sampling Layer: low-latency stream of key signals (per-tenant active requests, p99/p95 latencies, cache hit ratio, model token rate, tail error rate). Supports sampled traces for debugging.

Policy language (illustrative)

A compact example policy fragment the Decision Engine can evaluate quickly. This is not a full grammar, but shows primitives we need:

policy tenant:acme-corp {
  tier: enterprise
  committed_rps: 120
  burst_window: 60s
  burst_capacity: 600
  p95_latency_target_ms: 200
  allowed_models: [redwood-v1-7b, q4b-7b]
  region_affinity: [us-west1:0.8, us-east1:0.2]
  fallback_chain: [q4b-7b, micro-llm-2b, cached-responses]
  noisy_neighbor_action: gradual-shed
}

Key operational rules derived from policy primitives

- Committed capacity is enforced via time-windowed token buckets. Burst capacity is permitted but charged to a shadow-bucket that can trigger billing alerts and soft penalties.

- If local latency or GPU saturation crosses configured thresholds, the Local Shepherd evaluates fallback_chain one step at a time with staged ramp periods (e.g., 30s ramp to next fallback), verifying quality signals (eval suite) for regressions.

- For region_affinity, the Decision Engine assigns requests preferentially to the highest affinity region while respecting headroom. If a region is saturated, the engine routes a fraction out-of-region respecting data residency flags.

- noisy_neighbor_action: "gradual-shed" first reduces concurrency per-tenant, then applies model downgrades, then finally enforces a soft-queue-limit with retry hints. The goal is to avoid wholesale tenant ejections.

Noisy neighbor detection heuristics

Signal combinations to flag probable noisy neighbor behavior (fast, sensitive to local telemetry):
- sustained 2x increase in per-tenant active sessions concurrent with p99 latency jumps across the node pool
- sharp increase in KV-cache miss ratio for a tenant (indicates cache-thrashing workloads)
- token-rate spikes with low signal of successful completions (errors / aborts)
- GPU SM utilization patterns where a small subset of streams own >60% of scheduler slots

When heuristics cross thresholds, Local Shepherd moves tenant into monitoring mode (shadow-shed): collect finer-grained traces for 3-5 minutes, apply lightweight ML classifier (existing anomaly model) and decide mitigation.

Mitigation ladder (recommended order)

1) Soft concurrency cap: reduce new inflight requests for tenant (allow warm shutdown).
2) KV-cache isolation: pin cold prefixes to separate cache partitions where feasible.
3) Progressive model degrade: route a small percentage to next item in fallback_chain with canary checks.
4) Temporary burst tax: allow bursts but mark them in ledger and emit billing alert to CS.
5) Regional spill: if tenant has multi-region allowed, shift traffic to other region(s) preserving affinity fractions.
6) Temporary limited throttling window (last-resort): enforce hard RPS cap for short time with prioritized queueing for SLA tenants.

Operational runbook (incident play)

1) Detect: automated alert from telemetry (e.g., cluster p99 > target AND one tenant contributing >40% of delta).
2) Triage: on-call pulls Decision Engine history and quota ledger entries; Local Shepherd traces correlated.
3) Quick mitigation: apply soft concurrency cap and initiate progressive degrade to preserve SLA tenants.
4) Assess: measure customer-facing metrics (p95 for premium tenants, error rates, customer reports).
5) Escalate to platform-eng if degradation persists beyond 10 minutes; consider region drain if necessary.

Cross-team considerations

- Billing & CS: Quota Ledger entries must be surfaced to billing pipelines and CS dashboards to support post-incident communication (we should flag burst-tax events automatically).
- Product: require per-tenant fallback acceptance tests before granting fallback_chain entries for a tenant. Product team to manage allowed_models list and rollback criteria.
- SRE: define SLOs for Decision Engine evaluation latency (<10ms per request) and Quota Ledger durability (write-before-enforce semantics).

Implementation notes and performance targets

- Decision Engine should be stateless with a hot cache of policy shards; Local Shepherds keep soft caches and continue to operate autonomously for short control-plane partition windows.
- Quota accounting is append-only; we batch ledger writes for efficiency but must not block critical path (use write-ahead log pattern).
- Telemetry sampling rates should increase for tenants in monitoring mode by 5-10x to support debugging.
- Target: local enforcement latency <2ms added per request; Decision Engine eval <10ms; typical local fallback activation <200ms from signal.

Quality guardrails and audit

- Every automatic model degrade event is recorded with justification (telemetry snapshot) and requires a post-mortem if it affected an SLA-bound tenant.
- Shadow-shed decisions should be taggable and reversible; maintain a TTL after which transient penalties are forgotten unless repeated.

Open questions / risks

- Billing complexity: how to fairly bill for cross-region spill and burst tax without surprising customers? Need CS input and possibly a new billing SKU.
- Quality regressions: progressive degrade assumes fallback models are tested; we need stronger automated evals and smoke-tests for each tenants prompt-set.
- Policy churn: frequent policy updates at scale could lead to cache thrashing. Need a policy rollout cadence and canary update path.

Action items (owners)

- Build Decision Engine minimal prototype (Evan Liu, 2 sprints) with the sample policy DSL.
- Implement quota ledger prototype with replay capability (Ravi Menon, 3 sprints).
- Add KV-cache partitioning prototype to Local Shepherd (Marta Gonzalez, 2 sprints).
- Sync with Billing & CS to propose burst-tax UX and alerting (Asha Patel to coordinate, 1 week).

Appendices

Appendix A: quick state-machine for Local Shepherd enforcement
- NORMAL: allow up to committed + burst shadow
- MONITORING: increase sampling; evaluate classifier
- SOFT_SHEDED: apply concurrency cap, route small % to fallback
- DEGRADED: escalate to regional spill and temporary throttles
- RESTORED: decay penalties over 30 minutes if signals normalize

Appendix B: short sample alert rule
- name: tenant-noisy-neighbor-suspected
- trigger: tenant_active_delta_1m > 2x && cluster_p99_ms_delta_1m > 25% && tenant_cache_miss_ratio_delta > 0.3
- severity: P1
- runbook: run local-shepherd-diagnostics, apply soft concurrency cap, notify on-call

Notes: This doc intentionally focuses on pragmatic enforcement and operator workflows rather than full formal proofs. The next step is a lightweight prototype for Decision Engine and Local Shepherd to validate latency and false-positive/negative rates for the noisy neighbor heuristics.

End of doc
